hero.introParagraph: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric contact dermatitis (ICD-10 L25.9), including poison-ivy rashes, by secure video visit for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. A parent or legal guardian must be present and provide consent for every visit. Care centers on identifying and avoiding the trigger plus low- to mid-potency topical steroids for limited areas; TeleDirectMD does not prescribe oral or systemic steroids by telehealth and refers widespread reactions for in-person care. Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

telehealthRegulations.sectionTitle: Telehealth Regulations Across Our Licensed States
paragraphs: TeleDirectMD operates only where its physicians hold active licensure, currently 41 states plus Washington, DC. Each state sets its own telemedicine standards, and in every state a parent or legal guardian must consent to a minor's care. TeleDirectMD verifies that the child is physically located in a licensed state at the time of the visit; care is not provided to children outside the licensed footprint.

Some states limit telehealth prescribing of mid-potency topical steroids for pediatric contact dermatitis without an in-person follow-up. State-specific pages cite the controlling state statute. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

whatIsCondition.sectionTitle: What Is Contact Dermatitis in Children?
paragraphs: Contact dermatitis is skin inflammation caused by direct contact with an irritant or allergen. Irritant contact dermatitis (for example, from soaps or saliva) is most common, while allergic contact dermatitis (for example, poison ivy, nickel, or fragrances) is a delayed immune reaction.

It produces itchy, red, sometimes blistering skin in the pattern of the exposure and is managed with trigger avoidance plus topical anti-inflammatories. Per the American Academy of Dermatology contact dermatitis resources, identifying the causative agent is the most important management step.

TeleDirectMD focuses on limited contact dermatitis in children ages 5 to 17 that can be evaluated by video, with a parent present, and refers widespread or severe reactions, facial or eye involvement, and any signs of a severe allergic reaction to in-person or emergency care.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric contact dermatitis in children ages 5 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Irritants:
items.text: harsh soaps, detergents, saliva, urine, and friction can trigger irritant contact dermatitis.

items.label: Allergens:
items.text: poison ivy, oak, and sumac (urushiol), nickel, fragrances, and preservatives cause allergic contact dermatitis.

items.label: Materials and products:
items.text: rubber or latex, adhesives, and certain topical products can provoke a reaction.

items.label: Wet-dry cycles:
items.text: repeated wetting and drying, such as lip-licking or frequent hand-washing, can damage the skin barrier.

items.label: Exposure pattern:
items.text: the rash matches where the skin touched the trigger, a key diagnostic clue.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every rash is contact dermatitis. Atopic dermatitis (eczema), impetigo, ringworm, cellulitis, and hives can all look similar. TeleDirectMD uses history and the rash pattern to identify the likely trigger and directs atypical, widespread, or severe presentations to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Contact Dermatitis vs Eczema
compareCards.text: Contact dermatitis is triggered by direct contact with an irritant or allergen and appears in the pattern of that exposure, such as a streaky poison-ivy rash or a rash under a nickel snap. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing condition tied to a personal or family history of allergies, usually in the elbow and knee creases. The pattern and history distinguish them by video.

compareCards.title: Contact Dermatitis vs Impetigo, Ringworm, Cellulitis, and Hives
compareCards.text: Impetigo shows honey-colored crusting and is bacterial. Ringworm has a ring-shaped scaly border and is fungal. Cellulitis is warm, tender, spreading redness with fever and needs antibiotics in person. Hives (urticaria) are transient wheals that move and resolve within hours, unlike the fixed, exposure-shaped rash of contact dermatitis.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If there is facial or eye involvement, breathing difficulty, a widespread or severe reaction, or signs of infection, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person or emergency care.

treatmentOptions.intro: The most important step is identifying and removing the trigger. For limited rashes, a TeleDirectMD physician selects a topical steroid matched to the body site and adds an oral antihistamine for itch. Severe or widespread reactions are referred for in-person evaluation.

sections.title: Trigger identification and avoidance
sections.text: Identifying and avoiding the causative irritant or allergen is the most important step. For poison ivy, washing the skin and clothing promptly after exposure removes the urushiol oil that causes the rash.

sections.title: Topical steroids matched to the body site
sections.text: Low-potency hydrocortisone is used for the face and folds and mild cases, with mid-potency triamcinolone, fluocinolone, or mometasone for the body. Topical steroids are applied only to active rash for the directed time.

sections.title: Itch relief
sections.text: An oral antihistamine such as cetirizine can help with itch. Cool compresses and a fragrance-free moisturizer soothe and protect the skin while it heals.

sections.title: When to escalate
sections.text: Widespread or severe poison-ivy reactions that may need an oral steroid taper are referred for in-person care. Facial swelling, eye involvement, or breathing difficulty is a medical emergency. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe oral or systemic steroids by telehealth.

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Identify and avoid the trigger, and wash skin and clothing after a known exposure such as poison ivy.
Apply cool compresses and a fragrance-free moisturizer to soothe and protect the skin.
Use the prescribed topical steroid only on active rash for the directed time.
Trim nails and discourage scratching to prevent infection.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: If facial or lip swelling, eye involvement, or breathing difficulty develops, call 911.
If the rash becomes widespread or severe, seek in-person care for possible oral steroid therapy.
If the skin develops spreading redness, warmth, pus, or fever, watch for infection.
For poison ivy, new patches can appear over several days as the reaction develops.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Avoid the identified trigger going forward, and use barrier strategies when exposure is likely.
For poison ivy, the rash is not contagious once the oil is washed off.
Continue the prescribed topical steroid only for the directed time on active rash.
Return for in-person care for facial or eye involvement, widespread rash, or signs of infection.
Follow up by video if the rash is not improving as expected.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat my child's contact dermatitis online?
items.answer: Yes, for limited cases. TeleDirectMD treats contact dermatitis (ICD-10 L25.9), including poison-ivy rashes, by video for children ages 5 to 17 with a parent present. An MD identifies the likely trigger and prescribes a topical steroid plus an antihistamine for itch. The self-pay visit is $79, available in 41 states plus Washington, DC. Widespread or severe reactions are referred for in-person care.

items.question: How does a doctor identify the cause of contact dermatitis over video?
items.answer: TeleDirectMD physicians identify contact dermatitis in children ages 5 to 17 from the history and the pattern of the rash, which typically matches where the skin touched an irritant or allergen, for example a streaky rash from poison ivy or a rash under a nickel snap. The itchy, sometimes blistering rash in the shape of the exposure is the key diagnostic clue evaluated by video.

items.question: What does TeleDirectMD prescribe for pediatric contact dermatitis?
items.answer: For limited contact dermatitis in children ages 5 to 17, TeleDirectMD prescribes topical steroids matched to the body site, low-potency hydrocortisone for the face and folds, mid-potency triamcinolone, fluocinolone, or mometasone (ages 2+) for the body, plus an oral antihistamine such as cetirizine for itch. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe oral or systemic steroids by telehealth.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat my child's poison ivy rash?
items.answer: Yes, for limited rashes. TeleDirectMD treats poison-ivy contact dermatitis in children ages 5 to 17 with topical steroids and antihistamines when the rash is localized. Widespread reactions, or rashes involving the face, eyes, or genitals, may need an oral steroid taper and are referred for in-person care. Washing the skin and clothing promptly after exposure removes the urushiol oil that causes the rash.

items.question: When does contact dermatitis need in-person or emergency care?
items.answer: Seek emergency care if a child ages 5 to 17 has facial or lip swelling, eye involvement, or any breathing difficulty, which can signal a severe allergic reaction. See in-person care, not TeleDirectMD, for widespread or severe poison-ivy reactions that may need an oral steroid taper, or signs of skin infection. TeleDirectMD treats limited contact dermatitis online with topical therapy.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for a contact dermatitis visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any child ages 5 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD for contact dermatitis. The guardian's identity is verified, and the child must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the video visit.

items.question: Is contact dermatitis contagious?
items.answer: No. Contact dermatitis is not contagious; it is an inflammatory reaction to an irritant or allergen the skin touched. Even poison-ivy rash cannot spread to others once the urushiol oil is washed off, although new patches can appear over several days as the reaction develops. TeleDirectMD counsels parents of children ages 5 to 17 on trigger avoidance as the most important step.

items.question: How much does an online pediatric contact dermatitis visit cost?
items.answer: An online pediatric contact dermatitis visit at TeleDirectMD costs $79 self-pay, no insurance required, for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is in-network with Aetna, select Blue Cross Blue Shield plans, and UnitedHealthcare where applicable, but is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.

items.question: How is contact dermatitis different from eczema?
items.answer: Contact dermatitis is triggered by direct contact with an irritant or allergen and appears in the pattern of that exposure, while eczema (atopic dermatitis) is a chronic relapsing condition tied to a personal or family history of allergies, usually in the elbow and knee creases. A TeleDirectMD physician distinguishes them by video for children ages 5 to 17 from the rash pattern and history.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD treat contact dermatitis in children under 5?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD treats contact dermatitis only for children ages 5 to 17. Although topical steroids are used in younger children, TeleDirectMD's pediatric skin services begin at age 5. Children under 5 with a suspected contact rash should be evaluated by their pediatrician in person, especially when the trigger is unclear or the rash is widespread or near the eyes.

paragraphs: This page is informational and is not a substitute for in-person medical care. TeleDirectMD treats children ages 5 to 17 for contact dermatitis; we do not treat children under age 5 for any condition (ages 0 to 4 are excluded). A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent, and the child must be physically located in a licensed state (41 states plus Washington, DC) at the time of the visit.

TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances or isotretinoin, does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions or ADHD, does not make new asthma diagnoses, and does not prescribe oral or systemic corticosteroids by telehealth. Facial swelling, eye involvement, or breathing difficulty is a medical emergency: call 911. Any infant under 3 months with fever requires emergency care. TeleDirectMD is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.
